t: Three years to Mars and back. Nothing comes in, nothing goes out, and everyone has to eat.
A Mars mission is a closed system for about three years. Every atom of food, water and oxygen either goes with you or is made on board — and the mass you can launch is fixed before you leave.
sub: So everything has to go round.
Which is the distinction you drew in Ecology: energy flows through, matter cycles.

question: What is the hardest thing about keeping people alive for three years in a sealed can?
What is the binding constraint on a closed life-support system?
options: Everything has to be recycled, including the waste
stages.outcome: Everything has to be recycled, including the waste
note: Commit. Ask what a person consumes in a day, then multiply by three years and by the crew.

t: A closed system is a food web with nothing coming in. Take a level out and see what happens.
The same tri-trophic web from Ecology, standing in for a life-support system. Remove a level and watch how far the effect travels — because in a sealed vehicle there is no outside to buffer it.
goal: One thing goes and everything else changes. On Earth something else would cover it. On a ship, nothing does.
The cascade is the same one you measured before. What is different in a closed system is that there is no external input to absorb it — every effect is retained.

t: Pack the life support. Any part fits any slot, so the marking is on you.
Assign each element to what it closes. Placement is unconstrained, then it is stress-tested over three years.

label: Makes food and oxygen out of light
Turns yesterday's sweat back into drinking water
Takes out what everyone breathes out
Returns the nutrients so the plants can grow again
Means one failure is not the end

name: Breathe for a week
Air
pass: Carbon dioxide is removed as fast as it is produced.
CO₂ partial pressure held below the harmful threshold.
fail: Carbon dioxide builds up and the crew is unconscious in days.
This is the fastest-acting failure by a wide margin — days, not weeks.

name: Drink for three years
Water
pass: Closed-loop water recovery; the ISS already achieves over 90%.
fail: You would have to launch about a tonne of water per person.
Water is the heaviest consumable. Recovery is what makes the mass budget close at all.

name: Eat for three years
Food
pass: Plants produce food and oxygen together.
Photosynthesis closes food and contributes to air simultaneously.
fail: Stored food for three years is more mass than you can launch.
Food is the loop nobody has closed. No mission has yet grown a meaningful fraction of its own.

name: Keep the plants growing
Nutrients
pass: Waste is processed and the nutrients go back to the plants.
Nutrient cycling closes the loop; matter cycles because it cannot leave.
fail: The plants grew once and then ran out of nutrients, which are all in the waste tank.
Energy flows through and matter cycles. In a closed system, refusing to process waste means locking up the nutrients permanently.

name: Survive one thing breaking
Redundancy
pass: Functional redundancy across the critical loops.
fail: A perfect system, and one pump failure kills everyone.
This is the food-web lesson exactly: a system with one route per function is a chain, and every failure is fatal.

win: Air, water, food, nutrients and a spare for each. That is a biosphere you can launch.
All five. Note that the fifth is the same redundancy argument you met in Ecology, and that it is what turns a working system into a survivable one.
lose: Read which test failed — it names the loop that was open.
Each failed trial names the loop that was not closed. Reassign and re-test.

t: A system where everything goes round and nothing comes in is called closed.
A closed ecological life-support system recycles matter indefinitely, using only energy from outside. Earth is one; a spacecraft has to be built as one.
Energy crosses the boundary and matter does not — which is exactly the distinction from Ecology, made unavoidable by having a physical hull.

Nobody has ever closed one fully. Biosphere 2 famously failed on oxygen in 1991: concrete absorbed carbon dioxide and soil microbes consumed oxygen faster than anyone modelled, and the crew needed injections of outside air. The failure was informative rather than embarrassing — it was a flux nobody had thought to measure.
sub: Earth is the only one that has ever worked for long.
Every closed system built so far has needed topping up, usually with something nobody predicted would run short.
Which is a reasonable argument for treating the one that does work carefully.

It is also the strongest available demonstration of how little is understood about ecosystem-scale fluxes. We can sequence a genome and cannot yet build a sealed room that keeps eight people alive for two years without intervention.

q: Why must waste be processed on a spacecraft?
Why is waste processing not optional in a closed system?
Why does the matter-cycles principle become binding rather than merely true?
options: The nutrients the plants need are in it, and there are no others
It takes up too much room
why: There is no shop. Every atom the plants need to grow is already on board, and most of it is in the waste. Not processing it means locking those atoms away for the rest of the trip.

Matter cycles because it has nowhere else to go. The elements plants require are finite and on board, so any nutrient not returned is permanently removed from circulation and the food loop closes down.

On Earth the same principle is true and slack — the reservoirs are enormous relative to any flux, so nothing binds on a human timescale. In a sealed vehicle the reservoirs are the size of what you launched, so the cycle time becomes a hard operational constraint rather than a background fact.

t: Trying to build a small Earth is the best way anyone has found of noticing how the big one works.

Every attempt at closure has failed on something nobody was tracking — a gas absorbed by concrete, a microbial process nobody modelled. That is a genuine research method rather than a series of embarrassments: building a copy is how you find out which parts of the original you had not noticed.
